text: Every identity in an organization moves through three lifecycle events: joining, moving, and leaving. Identity governance teams call this the JML model - Joiners, Movers, Leavers - and it's the backbone of how access gets managed over a person's entire tenure, not just on their first day.

A joiner gets access provisioned for the first time, usually through a standard role-based bundle tied to their job title. A mover changes team, department, or role, and needs their access updated to match. A leaver's employment ends, and every credential tied to them needs to be revoked. The real risk with joiners is that whatever gets granted at onboarding quietly becomes the permanent floor - it's rarely re-examined after that first day.

Movers are the quietest source of access risk. When someone moves from Accounts Payable to Accounts Receivable, their new AR access gets granted fast, because withholding it blocks their work. Their old AP access almost never gets removed on the same timeline, because removing it doesn't block anyone - there's no urgency. After a few moves over a few years, an employee can accumulate a sprawling footprint of access nobody can fully explain. That's access creep.

Leavers are the highest-stakes event, and here's the real, common failure: Maria resigns as a database administrator. HR's termination process correctly disables her Active Directory account and email the same day. But she also had a SQL Server login a colleague created manually eighteen months earlier for a one-off project, and membership in a legacy file-server admin group - neither tied to her AD account, neither revoked. Both access grants survive her termination indefinitely.

Maria's case is exactly why mature organizations don't just trust the joiner/mover/leaver pipeline to catch everything - they run periodic access certification campaigns on top of it, because experience shows access granted outside the main pipeline reliably gets missed. That's where we're headed next: Lesson 22 covers how those campaigns work and what they're designed to catch.
